headline: Youth Development to hold exam with same committee despite question paper leak, sparking concerns
summary: The Youth Development Directorate is set to re-conduct the Upazila Assistant Youth Development Officer exam this Friday, even after the previous test was suspended due to a question paper leak. The same recruitment committee, whose role is questioned by some o
details: The Youth Development Directorate is set to hold the postponed exam for the Upazila Assistant Youth Development Officer position this Friday, October 16. This decision comes despite a recent question paper leak, with the same recruitment committee remaining in place, which some officials and committee members believe should be reformed to restore candidate trust.

The preliminary exam for 242 positions, attracting approximately 319,000 applicants, was originally scheduled for last Saturday across 98 centers in Dhaka. It was suspended shortly before commencement after leaked question papers circulating on social media were found to match the original.

The rescheduled exam is now set for October 16, from 3 PM to 4 PM. A five-member committee, led by Additional Secretary Mahfuzul Alam Khan of the Ministry of Youth and Sports, was formed to investigate the leak, but they have requested an extension and are yet to submit their report.

Several officials from the Ministry of Youth and Sports argue that the recruitment committee cannot evade responsibility for the question paper leak. One committee member also suggested that reforming the committee would convey a positive message to the candidates, though requests for some members to step aside were reportedly not considered.

Director General Motahar Hossain of the Youth Development Directorate stated that the perpetrators of the leak are still unknown, thus precluding immediate blame on the committee. He clarified that the Directorate lacks the authority to form a new committee, a decision that would require consultation with the Ministry of Public Administration and has not been made.

The five-member Divisional Recruitment Committee (DPC) for the Upazila Assistant Youth Development Officer post is chaired by Joint Secretary D.M. Atikur Rahman, who also serves as the Directorate's Director of Administration and Finance. Other members include the Deputy Director (Administration) of the Directorate, a Deputy Secretary from the Ministry of Youth and Sports, and representatives from the Public Service Commission (PSC) and the Ministry of Public Administration.

To enhance security and prevent further leaks, the Youth Development Directorate has altered the location for preparing and printing the question papers for the upcoming exam. The new papers will be prepared and printed on the night before the exam at the Ministry of Youth and Sports' conference room in the Secretariat, a change from the previous exam which was handled at the Directorate's Motijheel office.

Former Secretary and ex-Rector of Bangladesh Public Administration Training Centre (BPATC), Abdul Awal Majumder, noted that the government had the option to reconstitute the committee. He expressed confidence that the current recruitment committee would now be more vigilant following the incident, aiming to avoid any new controversies.

headline: Hilsa catch drops 12% in 2 years; public involvement crucial for conservation
summary: Bangladesh's Hilsa catch has significantly declined, prompting experts to advocate for community-led surveillance alongside government efforts to protect mother Hilsa during breeding season.
details: Despite a 22-day government ban on Hilsa fishing from October 8 to October 29, illegal fishing continues under the cover of darkness in remote char areas of the Meghna River. Fishermen are using current nets to catch mother Hilsa before dawn, transporting them to secret markets.

This unchecked activity is severely impacting Hilsa populations. The national Hilsa catch plummeted from a record 5.71 lakh tons in the 2022-23 fiscal year to 5 lakh tons in 2024-25, a 12% decline in just two years. Indiscriminate killing of Jatka (juvenile Hilsa) and mother Hilsa is identified as a primary cause.

Government surveillance faces significant limitations. The Fisheries Department's resources, including personnel and vessels, are insufficient to patrol the vast network of rivers, canals, and char lands across 165 upazilas in 37 Hilsa-dominant districts. Even with support from Naval Police, Coast Guard, and Navy, continuous presence at every ghat every night is impossible.

Evidence of illegal fishing persists, with reports from Patuakhali, Barguna, Tetulia, and Buragouranga rivers during the ban. Recent operations in Chandpur led to the arrest of 35 fishermen and the seizure of 50 lakh meters of current nets in a single night. In Patuakhali, 23 mobile courts conducted 93 raids in one day, highlighting the scale of the problem. A dolphin was also found dead in illegal nets during an operation in the Padma River in Shibchar, underscoring the threat to overall river biodiversity.

A past initiative, the EcoFish project (2014-2019) by the Fisheries Department and WorldFish, demonstrated the effectiveness of community involvement. It established co-management in 136 fishing villages near Hilsa sanctuaries, forming 575 Hilsa conservation teams and training nearly 400 community fish guards. This led to a bumper Hilsa production for four consecutive years from 2016 to 2019, proving that fishermen become the most effective guardians when they feel ownership of their resources.

Experts, officials, and fishermen representatives at a recent stakeholder meeting emphasized that public vigilance is indispensable alongside government operations for effective mother Hilsa conservation. Local communities possess crucial information about illegal activities, including which boats operate at night, which markets receive illegal fish, and where illegal nets are sold.

To address this, it is proposed to form volunteer 'Hilsa Guard Teams' in every fishing village and fish ghat. These teams would monitor rivers and ghats during the ban, particularly in remote char areas and branch rivers inaccessible to administrative vessels.

A direct communication channel, such as a hotline or dedicated mobile number, must be established between these public guard teams and law enforcement agencies like the Naval Police or Coast Guard. Prompt response to information and strict confidentiality for informants are crucial.

Incentives for participating fishermen are vital. Food aid should be provided before the ban begins, and members of the guard teams should receive honorariums, recognition, and priority for future government assistance. The state must support fishermen who protect the river despite their own hardships.

Surveillance must extend beyond the rivers to include fish markets, ice factories, fish transportation routes, and shops selling illegal nets, with local community oversight. Additionally, local councils, schools, college students, mosque imams, and local media should be engaged in awareness campaigns to foster a social stigma against illegal Hilsa fishing.
Finally, union-based data on operations, complaints received, and public involvement should be published after the ban concludes, ensuring transparency and accountability in conservation efforts.
